                                  INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF

          Pursuant to the March 18, 2026 Order Setting Procedural Schedule and Directing the

Filing Dates for Local Public Hearings (“Order Setting Procedural Schedule”), Google LLC

(“Google”), hereby files its Initial Post-Hearing Brief (“Initial Brief”). As further explained in this

Initial Brief, the Commission should (1) approve the LLPS Partial Stipulation and Agreement

(“LLPS Stipulation”) in its entirety without any modifications or changes and find that the

Stipulation and Agreement is just and reasonable and in the public interest, (2) reject modifications

to the Large Load Power Service (“LLPS”) Tariff proposed by the Office of the Public Counsel

(“OPC”) and (3) preserve the integrated framework for the Fuel Adjustment Clause (“FAC”),

thereby rejecting Staff’s proposals to impose separate, wholesale-market-based treatment of LLPS

customers.

 I. Introduction

              A. Google’s Interest

         1.      Google is a U.S.-based technology company that offers technology services and

products and operates multiple data centers in the country and around the world to power its

portfolio of products and services. Google is currently developing data centers in the Kansas City

area, including within Evergy’s service territory. Google’s energy spend will be directly impacted

by the outcome of this proceeding.

         2.      Google also participated in Case No. EO-2025-0154, which established the LLPS

Tariff (the “LLPS Tariff Case”). Google’s objective remains the same as in the LLPS Tariff Case:

to invest responsibly, to be a good community and grid partner, and to support a framework that

balances the opportunities of growth with meaningful protections for other customers.

              B. Procedural History

         3.      On December 8, 2025, Evergy Metro, Inc. d/b/a Evergy Missouri Metro (“Evergy”)

filed its Application in this docket, initiating a general rate case.

         4.      The following parties have been granted intervention in this proceeding: Midwest

Energy Consumers Group (“MECG”); Renew Missouri; Velvet Tech Services, LLC (“Velvet”);

Missouri Industrial Energy Consumers (“MIEC”); collectively the (“Intervenors”). Staff of the

Public Service Commission of the State of Missouri (“Staff”), the Office of Public Counsel

(“OPC”), and the Intervenors are referred to collectively as the “Parties.”

         5.      Pursuant to the March 18, 2026 Order Setting Procedural Schedule, on June 30,

2026, Staff and Intervenors filed Direct Testimony-Revenue Requirement; on July 14, 2026, Staff

and Intervenors filed Direct Testimony-Rate Design; on August 11, 2026, Evergy, Staff and

Intervenors filed Rebuttal Testimony; on September 10, 2026, Evergy, Staff and Intervenors filed



                                                   3
122214450.5
 Surrebuttal/True-up Direct Testimony; and on September 23, 2026, Evergy, Staff and Intervenors

filed True-Up Rebuttal Testimony.

         6.    On September 22, 2026, the Parties filed a Jointly Proposed List of Issues, Order

of Opening Statements, List and Order of Witnesses, and Order of Cross Examination (“Joint

Issues List”). On September 25, 2025, Google filed a Position Statement on the Joint Issues List.

         7.    The Parties held settlement discussions beginning on September 23, 2026 and those

discussions continued until evidentiary hearing, which began on the afternoon of October 5, 2026.

         8.    On October 5, 2026, shortly before the beginning of the evidentiary hearing, Google

and Evergy filed the LLPS Stipulation. The LLPS Stipulation does four primary things: (1)

recognizes the revenues from LLPS customers that are available now through a $60 million

revenue adjustment, (2) enforces the commitments already made in the LLPS Tariff by confirming

the operation of the minimum demand charge, (3) shares the benefits of growth with all customers

through an earnings sharing mechanism, and (4) it maintains the current structure of the FAC and

reserves any broader changes for an evidentiary record that can support them.

         9.    On October 6, 2026, Staff filed its Objection to the LLPS Stipulation. On October

7, 2026, OPC filed its Opposition to the LLPS Stipulation. On October 9, 2026, Evergy filed its

Support of the LLPS Stipulation.1

         10.   Between October 5 and October 13, 2026, the Commission heard live testimony

and argument during the evidentiary hearing and the “on-the-record presentation” regarding the

LLPS Stipulation and other partial stipulations addressing various issues in the case. On October

27, 2026, the Commission issued an Order Directing the Filing of a Joint Status Pleading and

II. Large Load Customers Provide Benefits to the Electric System But Only if They Remain
    a Part of the System

         12.   Evergy is a vertically integrated, rate-regulated public utility. “Vertically

integrated” means that Evergy owns all parts of an interconnected system of generation,

transmission and distribution required to serve its customers. Evergy plans its system through an

Integrated Resource Planning (“IRP”) process that accounts for all the needs of its system:

accounting for load growth, resource adequacy requirements, demand-side management

opportunities, and investments in established and emerging generation resources.2 Evergy also

incorporates all load, including LLPS customer load, into its resource commitments, market

positions, and participation in the SPP Integrated Marketplace.3

         13.   Google is an important part of this process and of Evergy’s integrated system. As

recognized in the Commission’s Report & Order in the LLPS Tariff Case, data centers are not just

large consumers of electricity, they are “economic and operational partners.”4 Findings 8 through

11 of the LLPS Tariff Order describe why: predictable energy use supports efficient planning and

demand management can strengthen reliability.5

         14.   The Commission also recognized the affordability benefit of large load customers.6

Consistent energy consumption spreads fixed costs over a larger volume of sales, contributing to

a lower average cost per kilowatt-hour.7 Google’s witness, Dr. Carolyn Berry, submitted testimony

that further explains these benefits.8 Large load customers do not merely add demand. They also

contribute revenues toward the shared system that serves everyone.9 Google takes its role as an

economic and operational partner seriously by working with utilities on demand-side flexibility,

long-term energy storage opportunities, advanced transmission technologies, and other grid-

strengthening and grid-improving initiatives. Those initiatives reflect Google’s approach to

helping the system become more capable, not simply asking it to supply more power.10

         15.   Staff and OPC have taken positions—both in the LLPS Tariff Case and this case—

that would partially or fully divorce large load customers from this integrated system. In this case,

this positioning is most starkly represented by Staff’s proposed “Option 2” for the Fuel Adjustment

Clause (or “FAC”).11 This positioning is also represented by OPC’s recommendation that all

CWIP-related costs of Mullin Creek #2 be allocated to LLPS customers, despite a lengthy record

         16.   Under Staff’s Option 2 for remaking the FAC (which is supported by OPC), LLPS

customers would be entirely removed from the FAC going forward. In order to back-out the costs

associated with LLPS customers from the FAC, Staff proposes using SPP wholesale market

locational marginal prices (“LMPs”) and matching those LMPs with LLPS customers’ load shape.

While Option 2 alone would not result in a complete separation of LLPS customers from the

integrated system, it would begin a process of attempting to isolate and directly assign discrete

pieces or costs of the integrated system to large load customers.16 The idea of separating LLPS

Customers from the rest of the system is taken even further by OPC in its position on Mullin Creek

#2 costs and in OPC’s and Staff’s recommendations regarding the expansion of the Interim

Capacity provisions of the LLPS Tariff.

          17.     The dangers of proceeding down a path of separate systems for LLPS customers

and others was recently articulated by the Staff of the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission:

         For over 100 years, the utility system has served all customers, and the cost of that
         system has been socialized amongst all customers to the shared benefit of all.
         Directly assigning new resources to only new large customers may erode that
         shared system and could potentially lead to a bifurcated system. One in which
         existing customers are stuck with aging equipment and another where new large
         customers benefit from a largely new grid with new generating resources. While
         allocating the costs for new resources to new customers may initially seem
         appealing to the wallets of existing customers, the consequences of splitting the
         system and allowing new large load customers to be excused from the ‘social
         contract’ of supporting the aging infrastructure of the broader system may prove
         detrimental to the customers that large load tariffs purport to protect.

         18.     From an operations standpoint, the advantages provided by data centers are

numerous. Data centers are consistent and predictable consumers of energy, which supports the

more efficient operation and planning of the electric utility grid.17 Data centers enable utility

system planners and grid operators to optimize existing generation and transmission infrastructure,

which can delay new infrastructure investments and improve overall system efficiency.18 Many

large load customers engage in demand management, which further enhances grid stability and

reliability.19

         19.     The economic advantage associated with data centers is that their consistent energy

usage helps distribute fixed costs across a larger energy volume, contributing to a lower average

cost per kilowatt-hour for all customers.20

         20.     Senate Bill 4 (“SB 4”) and the LLPS Tariff Order laid the groundwork for a clear,

objective, and transparent framework for infrastructure investment in Evergy’s service territory.

III. This is a Transition Case with No LLPS Customers in the Test Year

         21.       When the Commission established the LLPS Tariff, it established a clear, objective,

and transparent framework for infrastructure investment in Evergy’s service territory. The LLPS

Tariff fulfills the directives of SB 4, by ensuring large load customers bear their representative

share of costs and by preventing other customers’ rates from reflecting unjust or unreasonable

costs arising from service to such customers.

         22.       The LLPS Tariff only became effective in December 2025, which was also the last

month of the test year in this case. Accordingly, there are no LLPS customers in the test year for

this case, which runs from January 2025 to December 2025. The true-up period, which runs

through June 2026, only captures the beginning of a load ramp for one LLPS customer—it does

not reflect a reliable operating history from which to draw any conclusions.21

         23.       The signatories to the Non-Unanimous Global Stipulation and Agreement in the

LLPS Tariff Case (the “LLPS Tariff Settlement) recognized that the impact of LLPS customers on

cost allocation issues could not be evaluated until the first general rate case in which there is at

least one seventy-five megawatt (75 MW) or greater LLPS customer in the test year and captured

in the class cost of service (“CCOS”) study determinants.

         24.       Accordingly, at Paragraph 14 of the LLPS Tariff Settlement, the signatories agreed

to leave the Initial Pricing established by the LLPS Tariff Settlement in place until the first general

rate case which there is at least one 75 MW or greater LLPS customer in the test year, and further


         21
              Darrin Ives Rebuttal Testimony, at p. 11, ln. 6–12 (“Ives Rebuttal”).
                                                    9
122214450.5
 agreed to wait to evaluate the costs and impacts of any LLPS customers added to the system until

such general rate case.22 Further, Evergy agreed to track the premium paid by LLPS customers

compared to Large Power Service (“LPS”) customers until such a general rate case, and for CCOS

study purposes only, credit the premium to non-LLPS customer classes in determining the

sufficiency of class recovery of costs of service.23

         25.    This is not the case anticipated by Paragraph 14 of the LLPS Tariff Settlement.

Rather, this is a transition case with no LLPS customer data reflected in the CCOS billing

determinants. Without LLPS customer data reflected in the CCOS bill determinants, there is no

reliable way of evaluating LLPS customers’ relative contribution to the overall cost of service.

         26.    Nevertheless, non-LLPS customers are protected while a reliable operating history

is developed. Those protections include a twelve-year service commitment in addition to an

optional ramp period of up to five years; minimum demand obligations based on eighty (80)

percent of contract capacity; substantial collateral requirements; restrictions on capacity

reductions; and notice requirements and significant fees for early termination or contract capacity

reductions.24

         27.    Despite this being a transition case—with no large load customers in the test year—

other customer classes are already seeing the benefits of large loads in the form of a $60 million

revenue adjustment in this case. The $60 million revenue adjustment is discussed further below

in Section IV.A.

 IV. The Commission Should Approve the LLPS Stipulation because it Provides Meaningful
    Customer Protections and Reflects LLPS Revenues in this Rate Case

               A. The LLPS Stipulation Advances Affordability [Issues 3.A, 3.A.i]

         28.      Despite no LLPS customers in the test year for this case, under the LLPS

Stipulation, other customers will save $60 million per year as a direct result of LLPS customer

revenues. As noted by Evergy, this revenue adjustment is higher as a result of Google’s advocacy

for an interpretation of the minimum demand requirement in the LLPS Tariff that increases

Google’s monthly invoices. The LLPS Stipulation adopts Google’s position that billing demand

must be at least eighty (80) percent of annual contract capacity, with energy-based charges payable

in addition thereto.25

         29.      Specifically, Dr. Berry explained that the Demand Charge under the LLPS Tariff is

charged “Per kW of Billing Demand per month” and the “Billing Demand” is defined as “the

higher of (a) the Monthly Maximum Demand in the current month or (b) the Minimum Demand.”

The “Minimum Demand” is defined as “80% of the annual Contract Capacity.”26 Accordingly,

the Demand Charge is at a minimum equal to 80% of the Contract Capacity and is in addition to

the Customer Charge, Grid Charge, Energy Charge, DSIM Charge, and FAC Charge.27

         30.      Based on the corrected calculation of minimum monthly bills, annualized revenue

from LLPS Customers at the end of the true-up period equals approximately $60 million. Those

revenues offset the amount otherwise recovered from other customers, without any offsetting

LLPS costs in the rate base.

                B. The Proposed Earnings Review and Sharing Mechanism Balances Customer
                  Benefits and Evergy’s Incentive to Serve Large Loads [Issue 37]

         31.      The LLPS Stipulation addresses the anticipated growth in large load demand

following the establishment of rates based on a historical test year that did not include any large

load customers.28 Although some LLPS loads were reflected during the true-up period, most

anticipated growth will occur after the rates established in this case take effect.29 As a result, LLPS

revenues may increase faster than the costs reflected in the revenue requirement, potentially

causing Evergy’s earned return on equity (“ROE”) to exceed its authorized ROE.30 The LLPS

Stipulation proposes an earnings sharing framework that can balance protecting existing customers

and maintaining Evergy’s incentive to attract and serve large-load customers.

         32.      A transitional earnings sharing mechanism is supported by precedent in the recent

Ameren Missouri large load tariff case, File No. ET-2025-0184.31 In that case, the Commission

approved an earnings sharing mechanism providing that, when Ameren Missouri’s earned ROE

exceeds a certain threshold, the utility will retain thirty-five (35) percent and the customers will

receive sixty-five (65) percent, with fifteen (15) percent designated specifically for the benefit of

low-income customers. As Dr. Berry explained, “a similar sharing model could serve as an

effective transitional bridge that both aligns with recent Commission precedent and ensures a fair

balance of risks and rewards between Evergy and its ratepayers.”32

         33.      Under the LLPS Stipulation, Evergy retains its earnings up to twenty (20) basis

points above the authorized ROE. Earnings above that threshold are shared at sixty-five (65)

percent for customers and thirty-five (35) percent for Evergy. Although the LLPS Stipulation

         34.   The LLPS Stipulation reduces the customer-sharing percentage to sixty-five (65)

percent but also lowers the threshold to twenty (20) basis points, allowing customers to participate

in qualifying excess earnings sooner.34 This lower threshold partially offsets the reduced sharing

percentage, while Evergy’s retention of thirty-five (35) percent of qualifying excess earnings

preserves its incentive to attract and serve additional large loads. The negotiated mechanism

maintains the essential balance contemplated by Dr. Berry’s proposal—ensuring that customers

receive the majority of qualifying excess earnings resulting from large-load growth without

discouraging Evergy from pursuing large load growth.

         35.   The earnings sharing mechanism strikes a reasonable balance between protecting

customers and preserving Evergy’s incentive to attract and serve additional large loads. By

establishing objective criteria tied to the authorized ROE, actual LLPS revenues, and defined

sharing percentages, the mechanism promotes transparency and provides a clear, understandable,

and replicable framework for determining customer benefits.35 Ultimately, the LLPS Stipulation

ensures that customers have an opportunity to share in the financial benefits of large-load growth

while maintaining appropriate incentives for Evergy to pursue that growth.


V. Large Load Customers Mitigate Utility Risk and May Place Downward Pressure on the
   Cost of Equity [Issue 1.C]

          36.    The Commission should consider the risk-mitigating characteristics of the LLPS

Tariff when determining a fair return on common equity for Evergy. As Google witness Dr. Berry

explained, the Commission should weigh the mitigation of Evergy’s financial risks—associated

with both the stabilizing impacts of the LLPS Tariff and the strong investor interest in utilities

experiencing data center growth—as it seeks to balance utility and customer interests in this

proceeding.36

         37.    Specifically, the LLPS Tariff establishes a stable, long-term guaranteed revenue

stream for Evergy based on a minimum monthly bill utilizing eighty (80) percent of the contract

capacity regardless of the actual demand by the LLPS customer. It also requires collateral to

support this financial obligation and contains termination provisions that maintain revenues even

if the customer chooses to exit. This structure provides commercial protections that do not depend

upon the general economy, weather, or customer behavior. These features offer significant

financial stability which offsets large load risks.37

         38.    Moreover, where there is strong capital market interest in a particular sector, it can

create downward pressure on the cost of equity (and consequently the WACC) for companies

operating in that space. Past examples of this dynamic include digital infrastructure industries,

such as cell phone towers and fiber optic networks during the internet’s rapid expansion, and more

recently, the renewable energy sector amid the broader energy transition. In those instances, robust

investor demand helped lower effective equity costs and supported significant capital expansion.38

         39.    The Commission should weigh these dynamics—specifically, the credit-positive

impact of large loads, the financial protections embedded in the LLPS Tariff, and the strong

VI. Google Did Not Oppose the MECG-Evergy Rate Design Settlement Despite Its Original
    Position on LLPS Rates [Issues 30.A, 30.A.ii]

         40.   Google made a significant concession by not opposing the Non-Unanimous Partial

Settlement-Rate Design executed by MECG and Evergy on October 5, 2026 (the “Rate Design

Settlement”)39—under which the LLPS class is assigned 94% of the system average rate increase.40

         41.   Google maintains that it would be reasonable for the Commission to maintain the

LLPS Tariff rates at their existing levels, consistent with Dr. Berry’s recommendation to reject

Evergy’s proposed 15.19 percent LLPS rate increase, because the Commission only recently

approved the negotiated initial LLPS rates in the LLPS Tariff Case, and the present test year

contains no LLPS customers on which to base a class-specific cost of service determination.41

Despite these evidentiary concerns, Google recognizes the importance of its contributions to

Evergy’s integrated electric system, and therefore is not opposing the allocations set forth in the

Rate Design Settlement.


VII. The Commission Should Reject OPC’s Proposed Modifications to the Large Load
   Tariff because it Constitutes an Unsupported Collateral Attack on the LLPS Tariff
   Order [Issues 31.A, 31.B]

         42.   The Commission should reject OPC’s proposed changes to the LLPS Tariff. OPC

seeks to revisit central terms of a comprehensive tariff framework that the Commission approved

in LLPS Tariff Case less than a year ago. Its recommendations would lengthen the minimum

to ninety (90) percent of contract capacity, subject to a proposed performance offset; lower the

Usage Effectiveness (“PUE”), Water Usage Effectiveness (“WUE”), and Total Harmonic

Distortion (“THD”).42 These are not minor clarifications. They would materially revise the bargain

reflected in the Commission-approved tariff and impose new conditions on customers who are

making long-term investment decisions in reliance on that tariff.43

         43.   The Commission has authority to consider tariff revisions upon an appropriate

showing. But OPC has not made the showing necessary to justify these particular revisions in this

particular case. The LLPS Tariff Order was the result of extensive litigation and settlement

negotiations. That framework addressed eligibility thresholds, contract duration, minimum

monthly bills, collateral, termination and capacity-reduction protections, and reporting obligations

as interdependent components of a balanced package. Reopening selected components

immediately, without accounting for the protections in the package as a whole, threatens the

certainty that the Commission’s recent action was intended to provide.44

         44.   OPC’s proposal to extend the contract term to twenty years illustrates the defect in

its approach. Dr. Geoff Marke reasons that the twelve-year term may be shorter than the

depreciation life of resources developed to serve new loads and therefore could leave other

customers exposed if a data center departs. But the mere difference between a contract term and

         51.     In addition to not being supported by substantial competent evidence, Staff’s

proposal ignores the fact that Evergy operates an integrated system for all its customers, as

discussed above at Section II. Carving one customer class out of the FAC and treating it differently

is therefore discriminatory.

         52.     Staff’s proposal is also unworkable from an accounting perspective because it is

infeasible to isolate and attribute market outcomes (represented by LMPs) to a single customer or

class of customers.59 As explained by Evergy witness, JP Meitner, “market results are produced

through SPP’s centralized optimization processes, which are designed to identify the lowest-cost

and most reliable solution for the system as a whole rather than assigning specific market outcomes

to individual customers.”60 Mr. Meitner notes that attempting to isolate an individual customer’s

impact would require assumptions and allocation methodologies that do not reflect how costs and

benefits are actually created or realized within the SPP market.61

         53.     Moreover, the purpose of the FAC is to recover the variable cost of producing

energy, which is mostly fuel costs.62 As noted in Mr. Meitner’s Rebuttal Testimony, market results

(i.e., LMPs) are produced through SPP’s centralized optimization process and are not a proxy for

fuel costs.63 In fact, LMPs provide an incomplete picture about Evergy’s cost of producing energy

because Evergy sells the energy it produces into the SPP markets at LMP prices and buys the
